The villagers believed the forest was a clock, its trees ticking with the slow, patient pulse of time. Every century, the clock would need a new wound to remind it that life was fragile and precious.

On a night when the wind wore the scent of rain yet to fall, a girl named Aster wandered beyond the village’s edge and found a nest of glass eggs nestled in the roots of an elder tree. Each egg reflected a season—one held the hush of winter, another the bright ache of summer, a third the fever of spring, and the last the slow, tangled autumn. When she touched the eggs, they did not crack but sang, a chorus of possibilities. The eggs were promises waiting to be kept.

Aster carried them back, and the village elders gathered in the square. They spoke of balance: to receive the gifts of time, one must return something in kind. So they set the eggs on the village altar and offered their most cherished memory—of a night when the stars learned to listen. In exchange, the forest breathed anew, old wounds pinpricked by moonlight sealed, and the clock’s next tick began with a gentler pace.

From then on, every century, a child would be chosen to cradle a single glass egg, listening to its song, receiving the forest’s wisdom, and giving back a memory to keep time honest.
